lessons.title: Controlling facility utilisation
lessons.html:
Facilities as productive assets

Poultry houses, egg rooms, feed stores, generators, water systems and vehicles represent a large capital investment. Managing them well means keeping them productive for as many days as possible, at the right capacity, while protecting bird welfare, biosecurity and the life of the asset.

Utilisation measures

MeasureWhat it shows
House occupancyDays with birds divided by days available in the period
Output per square metreKilograms of meat or eggs produced per square metre per year
Turnaround timeDays from depletion to next placement, compared with the planned down time
Stocking levelBirds placed against the planned capacity
Equipment availabilityHours an item was available against hours it was needed

Finding lost capacity

Compare each house and each cycle. Common causes of lost days are slow clean-out because of too few people or a broken loader, late chick delivery, delayed repairs found only after depletion, and waiting for disinfectant to dry because cleaning started late. Under-stocking because of poor-condition drinkers or a weak fan also wastes capacity. Over-stocking is not a solution: it harms welfare and performance and may breach customer or welfare standards.

Controls

  • A site utilisation plan with placement dates and planned turnaround.
  • A turnaround checklist with responsible people and target days for each step.
  • Pre-depletion inspection so that repairs and parts are ready before birds leave.
  • Weekly review of occupancy and turnaround against plan.
  • Authorisation required for any change to house use or capacity.

Other facilities

Apply the same thinking to egg rooms and cold rooms, the feed store, staff housing and vehicles. Track usage, condition and cost, and decide whether assets are under-used, overloaded or due for replacement.

lessons.title: Managing maintenance and reporting on facilities
lessons.html:
A maintenance management system

Good maintenance is planned, recorded and reviewed. The aim is high reliability of critical equipment at a reasonable cost.

Elements of the system

  1. Asset register: every house and major item, with location, make, model, install date and service requirements.
  2. Criticality ranking: classify items by the effect of failure. Ventilation, water, power backup and alarms are critical because failure can kill birds quickly.
  3. Preventive schedule: calendar or hours-based tasks drawn from manufacturer manuals, such as generator services, fan belt checks, cooling pad cleaning and probe calibration.
  4. Job cards: every job, planned or breakdown, has a job card with the fault, work done, parts, hours and cost.
  5. Spares policy: critical spares kept on site; others ordered on lead time.
  6. Contractors: service agreements for specialist work such as electrical, gas and generator servicing, with proof of competence.

Safety and compliance

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 places duties on the employer for safe plant and machinery. Insist on lock-out procedures, permits for hot work and working at height, competent persons for electrical and gas work, and safety data sheets for chemicals. Keep fire extinguishers serviced and accessible. Never allow work on live electrical equipment or running augers.

Key maintenance indicators

  • Planned maintenance completed on time, as a percentage.
  • Number of breakdowns per month on critical equipment.
  • Downtime hours and any bird losses linked to equipment failure.
  • Maintenance cost per house or per bird placed against budget.

Reporting

A monthly facilities report should cover utilisation against plan, maintenance completed and outstanding, breakdowns and their causes, safety incidents, costs against budget and recommendations. Highlight assets that are failing repeatedly and present the case for repair or replacement with costs in rand and the risk of doing nothing. Owners can then make informed capital decisions.

Key points

  • Measure occupancy, turnaround and output per square metre to find lost capacity.
  • Prepare repairs before depletion to shorten turnaround.
  • Rank equipment by criticality and plan preventive maintenance.
  • Use job cards to record all work, parts and costs.
  • Report utilisation, maintenance, safety and costs monthly with recommendations.
